item.title: DAVID MARCUS: DAVID MARCUS: Egomaniac Fauci couldn't lie or plead 5th to his diary
item.description: Anthony Fauci pleaded the Fifth Amendment before Rand Paul's committee after his secret diary revealed doubts about COVID origins and mask mandates.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions on Capitol Hill Wednesday, but the humiliating release of his secret COVID-era diary just days before had already provided all the answers we needed about his demented ego and matchless mendacity.

Fauci short-circuited fireworks at the Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee hearing, run by his arch nemesis, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., by pleading the Fifth Amendment 111 times, even though he has a full pardon from the autopen of former President Joe Biden. But we had already heard plenty from him, thanks to the diary that was discovered on Fauci's government computer.

In early May 2020, we see Fauci musing that the "situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable," adding that he might be "the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable persons in the world."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

As a one-off, this entry might not be alarming, but in fact, the whole mini-memoir is filled with celebrities like Julia Roberts and CNN anchor Jake Tapper singing his praises in private, arranging A-list Zoom calls for Fauci, and generally venerating him as the greatest scientist on Earth.

It's an assessment he no doubt concurred with. After all, this is the man who once announced, when questioned over COVID lockdowns, "I am the science!"

According to Michael Caputo, who was the communications director for the Department of Health and Human Services, and who Fauci curses in his diary, "The very first time we discussed his TV appearances, Dr. Fauci waved all the red flags of a media hound. On my first day, he was already described as a problem."

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

It was this level of ego that allowed Fauci to write in his private diary on January 26, 2020, that "now we know the [wet] market was not the source, it was the amplifier," and the very next day say on television to the American people that the Coronavirus came from, you guessed it, wet markets. It had always strained credulity to believe that the deadly pathogen originated not in the mysterious laboratory where bat viruses were studied, but in a food market a stone's throw away. Now we know Fauci never bought the idea either. But he sure sold it.

Again and again, in his own words, we learn that privately he had serious doubts about not only the origin of COVID, but also the efficacy of masking, social distancing and the whole horrid host of shutdown measures that crushed our nation, while publicly insisting we must obey or we’d be killing grandma.

Fauci’s greatest sin, and what must now be his legacy, was his insistence on withholding information from the American people, and sometimes just flat-out lying, in order to make us behave as he thought we should.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Fauci and the Covidians had no desire for debate. In fact, they tried to destroy the careers of those who dared to question them.

The megalomaniacal picture of Fauci, in his own words, can be nothing short of infuriating for every American who suffered the indignity and often harrowing sorrow of isolation, all while he fought to silence scientists like Dr. Scott Atlas, who warned about the harm Saint Fauci was causing.

We must never forget how deranged Fauci followers, including governors such as Andrew Cuomo of New York and Gavin Newsom of California, became during this period, as kids lost years of learning through school closings.

Of course, they will all say, "We were just following the best science we had at the time." But let’s be honest: They wanted to put mask resisters in camps. They blew up schoolkids’ lives. They didn’t let you be with dying parents or have weddings. You couldn’t sing in the church choir. They tackled and arrested lone surfers on the beach. They made high school track athletes and band members wear masks while performing.

Those who bought into the hysteria and enforced the mad rules must forever be reminded of where they stood during that time, because otherwise it will happen again.

On Wednesday, a sad and defeated Fauci, far from the demigod of COVID times, sat stonefaced as Paul listed his lies. After each question, the disgraced doctor simply muttered, "On the advice of counsel I am invoking the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution."

For maybe the first time in his career, Fauci, who can spot a blinking red light at 200 paces, had nothing to say.

The bad news for Fauci is that his celebrity friends and loyal sycophants in the news media aren’t rallying around their former saint. It is far too late for that now. The best they can do is to just ignore it, pretending none of this is even happening.

For those of us who suffered under the iron fist of Fauci’s fallacious reign, and let's be honest that is everyone, there can be no forgiving or forgetting, only a deep, sharp anger.

Few, if any of us, will ever know what it is like to be heralded as a hero, as the sole voice of reason and science, for half of the country, to be worshiped with votive candles, and slobbered over by late-night "comedians."

We can’t know what that would do to us. But, we do know what it did to Dr. Anthony Fauci. It turned him into an abject monster.

item.title: Cubs vs. Cardinals pitching matchup between Matthew Boyd and Dustin May favors under 8 runs
item.description: Matthew Boyd's strong road ERA meets Dustin May's dominant home splits as the Cubs face the Cardinals in a matchup that points to under 8 runs.
item.content:encoded:
I took two losses on Monday in the games, with both of them ending 3-2. However, yesterday, I went 1-1 as I took the Marlins on the moneyline and Sandy Alcantara spun a gem for them. The loss was actually a win for a lot of people if they played just the moneyline. I got a bit greedy and played the run line, resulting in a loss. The Yankees won the game 3-2, but obviously didn't cover the run line. Three losses this week, all on games with a final score of 3-2. That's hard to do.

The Chicago Cubs are somehow making this team work. I'm a Cubs fan, so I have to give a bit of kudos to them because I assumed they were dead in the water when virtually every starter on their staff had been injured at one point or another. For now, the team is 61-46 with one of the better records in the National League. They aren't exactly one-dimensional, either. They can beat you with homers, or they can move station to station.

However, this team has been absolutely destroyed when it comes to pitching. They have a collective ERA of 4.20 and a WHIP of 1.27. Considering all of the injuries, those numbers actually aren't terrible. They've been getting good production out of today's starter, Matthew Boyd. For the year, Boyd is 6-1 with a 3.81 ERA and a 1.24 WHIP. Boyd has been solid on the road this season with a 3.21 ERA. Since his return from the injured list in June, he has made six starts and covered 35 innings. He has allowed just nine earned runs in those innings. Cardinals hitters are batting .267 against him in 30 at-bats.

The St. Louis Cardinals are having a better season than expected, but are still slightly below .500 at the moment. I don't expect them to make any big splashes this season, as they are probably ahead of schedule for their team development. They have a lot of young talent on the roster, and it doesn't make a ton of sense to abandon them via trade, or even add a ton of guys when they are just trying to develop and figure things out. Still, the Cardinals should be proud of where they are at currently, but know they have work to do if they want to get into the Wild Card race.

It would help for them to get some pitching if they want a true shot this season. Dustin May has been decent for them, but not great. For the season, May is 5-7 with a 4.59 ERA and a 1.32 WHIP. He is pitching in an optimal setting for him, though. He has a 3.45 home ERA and a 2.60 night ERA. Both are situations for tonight. In his last five home starts, he has 29.1 innings pitched and just six earned runs allowed. He hasn't faced the Cubs this season, but they are hitting .306 against him.

I am not sure I feel overly confident in fading Boyd at the moment, though. I also don't think May is a guy I want to fade in this spot. I'll lay off the sides.

item.title: Rand Paul seeks civil contempt charges after Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment more than 70 times
item.description: Rand Paul announced he will seek civil contempt charges after Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right over 70 times during the hearing.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director, left Wednesday's congressional grilling without answering lawmakers' questions, but Republicans are escalating their fight to compel his testimony.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday that he will seek civil contempt charges against Fauci after he invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 70 times during the blockbuster hearing.

"We're going to have a vote next week on contempt. I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon," Paul said. "And that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity."

The planned committee vote is likely to be along party lines as several Democrats on the panel came to Fauci’s defense on Wednesday.

Paul, the top Republican on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, subpoenaed Fauci to testify about the origins of COVID-19 after he declined to appear voluntarily.

Fauci repeatedly pleaded the Fifth, arguing Paul had an "obsession" with seeking his arrest and released more than 1,000 pages of his "personal diary" over the weekend in an effort to embarrass and intimidate him, according to his opening statement.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Red state governor pummeled online after defying Trump’s deportation orders
item.description: Gov. Mike DeWine called Haiti "hell" while arguing against deporting Haitian TPS holders, sparking fierce online backlash from critics on social media.
item.content:encoded:
A Republican governor in a state that voted to elect President Donald Trump is facing intense backlash online after an interview arguing against the president's order to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) migrants from the United States.

Republican Gov. Mike DeWine's state is home to an estimated 30,000 Haitian TPS holders. He told CBS earlier this week that the Haitians shouldn't be sent back to their country of origin.

"Haiti is hell today. So you'd be sending people … back to hell," he said. "Very few of these Haitians will voluntarily go back to Haiti. If they have to leave, they'll go someplace else. They want to work. They want to support their family. They don't want to go back to Haiti."

BLUE STATE LEADERS ERUPT AFTER SUPREME COURT’S DECISION ENDING TPS PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIANS, SYRIANS

Online detractors quickly seized on DeWine's comments, mostly from users claiming that those responsible for Haiti's conditions are the ones that the governor wants to allow to stay in the United States.

"What makes Haiti hellish? Is it…the Haitians?" asked Sean Davis, co-founder of The Federalist, in response to CBS' story about the interview posted on X.

"Hey governor, what is it that makes Haiti so bad anyway?" The Blaze's Logan Hall asked.

"I think the real question here is, if Haiti is hell, why are we importing Haitians?" questioned internet personality Larry Sanger.

TRUMP'S 'THIRD WORLD' TRAVEL BAN COULD BECOME PERMANENT IF FIREBRAND REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER GETS HER WAY

Others referenced the liberal media's freakout when, in 2018, Trump referred to Haiti and some other nations as "s---hole" countries.

Meanwhile, TV personalities and talking heads, comedian Conan O'Brien chief among them, defended Haiti for its natural beauty.

"Still reeling from [Trump's] very negative Yelp review of Haiti, which means I'll love it," O'Brien said at the time, announcing a trip to the country. "I have no idea what the president has against the people of Haiti, but if the president doesn't like them, they must be lovely people."

DEM-LED PUSH TO EXTEND PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIANS FACES OUTRAGE AFTER BRUTAL HAMMER KILLING

One X user specifically blamed Haitians for DeWine's characterization that the country is "hell."

"Or is it a paradise like so many celebrities have said?" the user asked.

"I was reliably informed by democrats [sic] and hollywood [sic] celebrities that Haiti is utopia," said another user.

"What a tragedy it would be for Haitians to live in Haiti," said another X user.

DeWine argued in the CBS interview that sending Haitians back to Haiti would be a "mistake" that would endanger the lives of the TPS holders.

He also specifically mentioned Springfield, his hometown, which has a large population of Haitian TPS holders.

"These are people who have helped Springfield really come back," DeWine said. "The Haitians who are living there and employed there, they came there to work, and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people."

TPS was officially terminated Monday after Trump's order survived a Supreme Court review.

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that — temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent," a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Fox News Digital earlier this week.

TPS was created as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, and was designed for people facing serious emergencies like armed conflict or severe natural disasters. Critics claim it has been abused to give status to those in the U.S. for non-emergent reasons.

DeWine's office declined to comment on "statements made in online comment sections," when reached by Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

Fox News Digital's Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Landon Donovan 'disappointed' Folarin Balogun red-card fiasco got 'out of hand' after Trump's involvement
item.description: Landon Donovan says the Folarin Balogun red card controversy "tainted" the USMNT's incredible World Cup run and motivated Belgium ahead of their match.
item.content:encoded:
Hindsight is 20/20, but it sure seems like Landon Donovan wishes the Folarin Balogun red-card controversy just played itself out.

The USMNT star received a red card in the round of 32 of the World Cup, which initially made him ineligible to play in the next round. However, FIFA decided to suspend the red card, which made Balogun eligible. President Donald Trump later said he called FIFA President Gianni Infantino and asked for a review, but FIFA claimed it was not influenced by Trump.

Nonetheless, the ruling added to what was already a huge controversy, and Donovan said the situation got "out of hand."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"I was disappointed... because it had been a World Cup full of nonpartisanship — people just loving America, loving the flag and loving what they were watching. Then it became very messy, and nobody wanted to see that, because we love the sport. We loved what we were watching, and the players have since admitted that it became difficult for them," Donovan told Fox News Digital in a recent interview. "It tainted what had been an incredible run.

"The really sad part is that it never should have been a red card, but that is the reality. It's just disappointing that it got out of control that way. I felt bad for Balogun. I felt bad for the team, to be honest, and it was very clear that it motivated the Belgian team."

The International Olympic Committee recently said it was not investigate Infantino regarding Trump's call to him.

IOC DECLINES TO INVESTIGATE GIANNI INFANTINO OVER TRUMP'S CALL ABOUT FOLARIN BALOGUN RED CARD

"All I did was I asked for a review because I didn’t think it was a foul," Trump said at the time. "And, again, I’m good at this stuff. I didn’t think it was a foul. I thought it was two great athletes who crashed into each other and got entangled. That was not a guy punching somebody in the face or anything, that would be different.

"I think it’s a terrible … if they wouldn’t allow a top player, maybe the best, maybe among the best on the team, to play. I think it would have had a big stain. I relayed it. I didn’t tell him what to do. I don’t believe he made the decision. I think it was a committee that made the decision, and they made the right decision because, No. 1, it wasn’t a foul, and you want to see a game with your best players."

As Donovan noted, Balogun admitted that the red card fiasco resulted in "a lot of outside noise" and caused "quite a bit of nerves" among the team.

"The closer we got to the game, I tried to just focus as best as I could, but it was difficult. A lot of outside noise and that’s hard to avoid," Balogun said earlier this month.

Belgium gave a strong response to Balogun being eligible for the game, but to no avail. At the end of the day, though, they got the last laugh with a 4-1 victory.

item.title: Why the under is the play as Trevor Rogers and Tarik Skubal face off in Baltimore-Detroit matchup
item.description: Tarik Skubal takes the mound in what could be his final Tigers start before the trade deadline as Baltimore's Trevor Rogers rides a hot streak.
item.content:encoded:
The trade deadline is looming, but that doesn't mean we are going to take our foot off the gas. I did mention it is smart to lower your unit size a bit on some of the baseball bets for the next couple of weeks, and I stand by that. You never know who will be part of a blockbuster trade, and you don't want your money tied up into something that isn't all that predictable. There isn't a bigger name available than the guy who is making a start today as the Orioles take on the Tigers.

The Baltimore Orioles season hasn't exactly gone to plan. They added Pete Alonso, and he has been a rewarding free agent, but the team is still hitting just .237 for the season. The pitching staff has a 4.21 ERA and a 1.35 WHIP. In the ultra-competitive American League East, there just isn't much room for error. They enter today's contest with a 52-56 record, which isn't terrible, but does probably put them in the seller conversation more than the buyer's room.

There is a lot of talent on the Orioles, but you have to wonder how they adjust for not only the remainder of this year, but next year too. They need help in the rotation, but their bullpen, a strength for so long, has actually been very good for the last couple of months. Maybe that's something to hang their hats on. Trevor Rogers takes the hill today with a 6-7 record, a 4.17 ERA, and a 1.27 WHIP. He's been fine, but nothing special. He has been better on the road than at home, with a 3.72 road ERA, and he has been great the past two months with just 11 earned runs allowed in 55 innings. Tigers hitters are batting .270 against him in 37 at-bats.

The Detroit Tigers are at a significant crossroads, and they also did not have this season go the way they intended. They will have plenty of people calling about a variety of their players. Their offense seems to have improved from last year, and their pitching looks about the same, but they haven't progressed from the slump they had to close last season. They are six games under .500 for the year and haven't played very well on the road this year.

As mentioned, no one will garner more attention than the man who takes the mound today for Detroit, Tarik Skubal. If you follow baseball at all, you know he is in the prime of his career, about to be a free agent, and has won the past two Cy Young awards. His numbers are still strong this year despite missing some time with injury. He is 7-5 with a 2.70 ERA and a 0.92 WHIP. He has been worse at home than on the road with a 3.46 home ERA. He has been his typical dominant self in July with a 1.48 ERA this month.

You do have to wonder if this is the last start that Skubal will make for the Tigers. If they don't trade him, they will let him walk for nothing as they are likely very far apart on a contract. Starters like this don't come around often, and the return has to make it worthwhile even if the Tigers still think they can make the postseason without him this year.

item.title: Controversial teacher training targets parental authority as oppression, education expert warns
item.description: PragerU CEO Marissa Streit warns that "adultism" concepts in ethnic studies curriculum are being used to undermine parental authority in 22 states.
item.content:encoded:
Teacher training programs across the country are adopting radical new educational theories to undermine parental authority and drive a wedge between parents and children, PragerU CEO Marissa Streit warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Streit is raising concerns over the rapid spread of the "ethnic studies" curriculum, which she says is being implemented or endorsed in more than 22 states across the nation. She specifically cited the controversial term "adultism," saying it paints standard parental boundaries as a form of oppression.

While the term "adultism" historically originated in sociology to describe age discrimination against children, Streit argued it has found new life in teacher training materials and is being used to portray standard parenting rules on clothing, relationships or major medical decisions as a form of "fascism" or tyranny.

FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS

Streit displayed a teacher training manual titled, "Lessons In Liberation: An Abolitionist Toolkit for Educators," which she says promotes anti-capitalism, Critical Race Theory (CRT), and the rejection of adult authority.

The textbook's publisher, AK Press, says the book is "designed for educators, parents, and young people, this toolkit shines a light on innovative abolitionist projects, particularly in Pre-K–12 learning contexts."

However, Streit argues that ethnic studies modules simply repackage concepts like DEI, social-emotional learning, and Critical Race Theory, that have received negative attention, to promote many of their same anti-capitalist and Marxist ideals.

TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

"[Ethnic studies] teaches the teacher to tell the student that the term adultism is a negative thing," Streit told Fox News Digital. "When an adult is behaving like an adult by telling their child that the child should not dress a certain way or have sex at an early age or even request sex or gender changes ... the parent is engaging in adultism." 

She quoted a passage from the text, which allegedly says, "Adultism teaches us that adults have the power and the right to decide what young people's boundaries should be."

According to a June report by the San Francisco Chronicle, ethnic studies workshops at local schools have drawn "significant controversy" for promoting the idea of adultism as a form of oppression.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

item.title: Oscar-winning singer Glen Hansard dead at 56
item.description: Glen Hansard, the Oscar-winning Irish singer-songwriter behind "Falling Slowly" and star of "Once," died at 56 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
item.content:encoded:
Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard, the Academy Award-winning musician behind the beloved song "Falling Slowly" and star of the acclaimed film "Once," has died after a motorcycle crash in Dublin. He was 56.

Hansard's management confirmed his death Wednesday, telling Irish broadcaster RTÉ that his family was "deeply shocked and heartbroken."

According to Irish police, a man in his 50s was killed in a single-vehicle motorcycle crash in Lucan, on the outskirts of Dublin, before 4:30 a.m. Wednesday. First responders treated the rider at the scene, but he was pronounced dead shortly after.

'IT TAKES TWO' RAPPER ROB BASE DEAD AT 59 AFTER CANCER FIGHT HE KEPT HIDDEN FROM FRIENDS

Hansard's legacy was tied to "Once," the 2007 Irish musical drama that transformed him from a respected hometown musician into an international star.

Starring opposite Markéta Irglová, Hansard played a struggling street musician whose connection with a fellow artist unfolds through music on the streets of Dublin.

The film became a global success, earning roughly $23 million at the worldwide box office and producing one of the decade's most memorable original songs, according to Rolling Stone.

GEORGE MICHAEL DIED WORTH $128M, BUT FRIENDS SAY HE SECRETLY GAVE AWAY MILLIONS FOR DECADES: AUTHOR

Hansard and Irglová won the Academy Award for best original song in 2008 for "Falling Slowly," a quiet acoustic ballad that became synonymous with the film.

Long before Hollywood recognition, Hansard had already established himself as one of Ireland's most respected performers.

Born in Ballymun, Dublin, in 1970, he began playing music as a teenager while busking throughout the city. 

In 1990, he founded The Frames, a band that developed a devoted following over several decades. Around the same time, Hansard expanded into acting, appearing as guitarist Outspan Foster in Alan Parker's 1991 film "The Commitments."

His career continued to evolve after "Once." Alongside Irglová, he formed The Swell Season while also maintaining an active solo career.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

His 2015 album "Didn't He Ramble" earned a Grammy nomination for Best Folk Album.

Hansard was equally recognized for the way he remained connected to Dublin's music community despite his international success.

Each Christmas Eve, he gathered fellow musicians outside Dublin's Gaiety Theatre for a charity busking tradition benefiting the Dublin Simon Community, an annual event that became a holiday fixture for locals.

He also played a prominent role during one of Ireland's most emotional public farewells.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

At the funeral of Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan in December 2023, Hansard and Irish singer Lisa O'Neill performed "Fairytale of New York," inspiring mourners throughout the church to sing and dance in celebration of MacGowan's life.

Hansard's reputation reached well beyond Ireland.

The Irish musician joined Bruce Springsteen onstage at Kilkenny's Nowlan Park in 2013 for a performance of "Drive All Night."

Tributes from across Ireland began pouring in within hours of news of his death.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin wrote on X that he was "deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Glen Hansard."

"A talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland's cultural landscape over many years," Martin posted.

Waterboys frontman Mike Scott also reflected on Hansard's legacy, writing on X, "Just heard that Glen Hansard has died. Travel on well, Buddy. You made your dreams come true. I'm so sorry that he leaves his wife and 3-year-old child."

Hansard is survived by his partner, Finnish poet Maire Saaritsa, and their son, Christy, who was born in 2022.

His career leaves behind a catalog that stretched from Dublin sidewalks to the Oscar stage, making him one of Ireland's most enduring musical voices.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrat compares ICE to 'domestic terrorists' as 111 House Dems demand Texas detention center close
item.description: House Democrats panned the Trump administration's immigration crackdown after a visit to a Dilley detention center in Texas.
item.content:encoded:
A House Democratic lawmaker compared actions by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to domestic terrorism after a visit to a Texas detention facility on Tuesday.

Rep. Luz Rivas, D-Calif., said that seeing ICE's actions was personal for her as the daughter of Mexican immigrants and argued that "for the people of the United States, we don't want to see our government, or ICE officials, acting like domestic terrorists," she said in Spanish during a press conference.

She said her Los Angeles district saw more ICE raids than anywhere else in her county.

Rivas was among a group of lawmakers led by Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on a visit to an ICE facility in Dilley, Texas, which over 100 House Democrats have demanded to be shut down.

TRUMP ON VERGE OF SECURING $70B ICE FUNDING VICTORY AFTER HOUSE CLEARS HURDLE

The lawmakers accused the Trump administration of holding families, including a child as young as 2 months old, in inhumane conditions.

Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., a member of the left-wing "Squad," also attacked President Donald Trump as a "dictator."

SOMETHING TO HIDE? ICE UNDER FIRE FOR SUBSTANDARD CONDITIONS AT FOR-PROFIT DETENTION CENTER

"It's so important that we not acquiesce to this, this fascist administration, this dictator in the Oval Office," Pressley said. "History has shown us time again, appeasement does not work. The only way to beat a dictator is with defiance. The only way to beat fascism is to refuse to accept this segregated, divided, dark, dystopian view that they have for our country, is to reject it as an inevitability."

She called on Americans to "resist, reject, condemn at every turn."

But it's that kind of rhetoric that Republicans have argued is responsible for sending tensions across the U.S. skyrocketing.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to Rivas' comments, "Attacks and demonization of ICE law enforcement are wrong. Because of smears like this our ICE officers are now facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line to arrest murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists. ICE law enforcement is arresting criminals and saving countless American lives."

"Rep. Luz Rivas should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her state—NOT vilifying law enforcement," the spokesperson said.

SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS

GOP allies of the president have accused Democrats of encouraging violence and resistance against ICE agents, drawing a line between encouragement to resist federal immigration officers and the slate of violent incidents involving those officers this year alone.

But Democrats are accusing ICE of acting as a rogue agency outside the bounds of the law.

"We have to abolish ICE. And then I'm going to take it one step further and say any of those agents that have contributed to and caused the injury, the harm, and even fatalities, they must also be held accountable," Pressley said. "And we should abolish qualified immunity for these federal law enforcement officers."

In a letter sent earlier this month, 111 House Democrats accused the administration of harming children and families with the conditions at the Dilley detention center.

"Parents describe horrendous conditions at Dilley, leading to severe depression, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation amongst their children. Children have reported that their food is often contaminated with worms and mold and that they feel sick after drinking tap water," the letter said. "Families also report not being able to sleep at night because the lights are kept on in their rooms throughout the night. … Medical care provided by CoreCivic staff is delayed, denied, and in many cases outright dismissed, even when children are suffering life-threatening medical emergencies."

DHS did previously accuse Democrats of lying about conditions at Dilley, which it said in a press release was specialized to hold families and care for children specifically.

"The Dilley facility is retrofitted for families. Children have access to teachers, classrooms, and curriculum booklets for math, reading, and spelling. They have access to age-appropriate books, toys, and outdoor activities. All of this is generously funded by the U.S. taxpayer," DHS said.

"Infant care packages include formula, baby food, bottles, diapers, wipes, and hygiene items. The facility also provides sippy cups and cribs. Adults with children are housed in facilities that provide for their safety, security, and medical needs."

item.title: Close call at Atlanta airport forces Delta anti-collision alarms to sound
item.description: Cockpit alarms blared as two Delta Air Lines jets crossed paths during a go-around at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport, now under FAA investigation.
item.content:encoded:
Cockpit alarms blared as two Delta Air Lines jets narrowly avoided each other over Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport during a frightening near miss now under federal investigation.

The incident between the two Delta flights happened around 11 p.m. Monday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"Delta Air Lines Flight 2472 was departing from Hartsfield – Jackson Atlanta International Airport when it crossed in front of Delta Air Lines Flight 1568, which had executed a pilot-initiated go-around because another aircraft was slow to exit the same runway," the FAA said.

FAA INVESTIGATES AFTER INCOMING PLANE EXECUTES GO-AROUND DUE TO AIRCRAFT LEAVING FROM INTERSECTING RUNWAY

On-board, anti-collision warning systems sounded in the cockpit as one pilot could be heard uttering, "My goodness," according to air traffic control audio obtained by CBS News.

Delta told Fox News Digital in a statement that the maneuver was in accordance with established procedures and that its crew undergoes extensive training for these types of uncommon scenarios.

AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL AUDIO CAPTURES TENSE MOMENT TWO PLANES NEARLY COLLIDED AT BOSTON LOGAN AIRPORT

"As safety remains at the core of everything we do, the crew of Delta Flight 1568 performed a go-around during approach into Atlanta due to potential traffic on the runway," Delta said. "During the go-around, the crew maneuvered in accordance with established procedures to maintain separation from other air traffic."

The airline said that the flight landed safely and passengers deplaned normally.

The FAA said the incident is under investigation. Delta said it will fully cooperate with authorities on any review.

item.title: Cannabis cafes may become tourist draw in US city as lung experts cite 'toxic chemical' concerns
item.description: San Francisco's Board of Supervisors voted to allow Amsterdam-style cannabis cafés serving food and nonalcoholic drinks at licensed retailers. Health experts have concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Amsterdam-style cannabis cafés are one step closer to opening in a major U.S. city — with others potentially watching closely. 

The San Francisco Board of Supervisors voted in mid-July to allow licensed cannabis retailers to serve food and nonalcoholic drinks on site — similar to cannabis cafés that exist in the Netherlands, as Fox 2 KTVU reported. 

Even as retailers anticipate pulling in more tourist traffic as a result of the development, lung experts cite health concerns connected to the move. 

ONE CANNABIS MISTAKE AT AIRPORT COULD BRING 10 YEARS IN PRISON AND $15,000 FINE

Under the new ordinance, cannabis may only be consumed on the premises and cannot be taken off-site. Alcohol and tobacco, meanwhile, are prohibited.

Operators must also obtain a Department of Public Health consumption permit alongside their Office of Cannabis permit, meet restaurant food safety standards and electronically verify every customer's age at the door.

The measure supports AB 1775, a 2024 state law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom that allows cities to issue licenses for cannabis cafés, as local outlet KQED reported. In a statement, Rafael Mandelman, board president, said San Francisco "just gave our legal cannabis industry a real tool to compete and grow," the outlet reported. 

He also cited the potential economic benefits of attracting more visitors.

Mayor Daniel Lurie, a Democrat, signed the legislation July 23. On August 23, the Office of Cannabis will begin accepting applications for cannabis café permits.

SMOKING AND VAPING MAY BE BANNED AT ONE STATE'S MOST POPULAR BEACHES AND PARKS: HERE'S WHY

The passage of the cannabis café legislation "marks a new initiative for the city’s economic recovery and for the broader cannabis community," said Nikesh Patel, director of the San Francisco Office of Cannabis.

Patel's office "is working closely with other city departments to implement this new permit type responsibly, while maintaining core services to enforce compliance across the industry," he told Fox News Digital.

Amy O'Gorman Jenkins, executive director of the California Cannabis Operators Association, told Fox News Digital she thinks other cities "can and should consider similar models," assuming San Francisco's experiment is a success.

"The purpose of authorizing cannabis cafés was to transform a brief retail transaction into a hospitality experience," she said.

WORLD’S MOST BEAUTIFUL AIRPORT CROWNED AND IT’S RIGHT HERE IN THE UNITED STATES

"Allowing this activity in San Francisco will attract visitors … and generate broader economic activity," she asserted.

O'Gorman Jenkins said cannabis cafés "are not simply dispensaries where people can stay longer."

O'Gorman Jenkins mentioned that AB 1775 has safeguards to protect employees from excessive secondhand smoke — but not everyone agrees. 

A representative from the American Lung Association told Fox News Digital the ordinance moves San Francisco "in the wrong direction" because of secondhand smoke.

"Permitting cannabis lounges normalizes [the] deleterious effects of smoking cannabis and exposes the adjacent properties to secondhand cannabis smoke, which contains many of the same toxic chemicals, carcinogens and fine particulate matter found in tobacco smoke," said Kesa Bruce, director of California Advocacy for the American Lung Association.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Employees working in cannabis cafés would be required to spend hours each day in an environment where they are repeatedly exposed to harmful airborne pollutants simply to do their jobs," Bruce contended.

"There’s a widespread belief that marijuana is ‘natural’ and therefore harmless," Corey Gamberg, a mental health and addiction specialist who serves as executive director of the Rockland Recovery Center and Massachusetts Center for Addiction, previously told Fox News Digital.

"In reality, today’s products are far more potent than in previous decades, and we’re seeing very real mental, emotional and physical consequences in clinical settings every day."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Trent Carter, a board-certified nurse practitioner, addiction recovery expert and founder of Renew Health, an outpatient treatment center in New Mexico, also noted that marijuana has become a more commonly accepted substance — but he's seen some negative effects in his own patients.

"As time went on, I discovered that the vast majority used marijuana to treat a number of mental and physical issues, only to induce a litany of other symptoms as a result," he told Fox News Digital earlier this year.

The proposal sparked discussion on a San Francisco Reddit forum, where users expressed excitement.

"This is sooooo needed. Can’t wait," a commenter wrote.

"I'll be seeing you guys there in 10 years when the first café finally opens!" another joked.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Others were skeptical about the plans.

"I hope this [will] limit some public weed smoking," one person said. "It’s such an anti-social behavior. Don’t like getting hit with other people’s big puffs out on the street."

Another person wrote, "It would be nice to have more social spaces, but the indoor smoke makes them pretty much un-attendable for more than a few minutes."

The proposal also comes as cannabis increasingly intersects with the travel industry.

Earlier this month, officials reminded Americans that bringing cannabis products across international borders remains illegal in many countries, warning travelers that even legal purchases made in the U.S. lead to steep fines or prison sentences abroad.

Melissa Rudy of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: LIV Golf reportedly canceling its finale makes CEO's comments about 'incredible' Saudis look wildly foolish
item.description: Multiple contractors reportedly say travel and accommodations were cancelled as LIV Golf's $40 million team championship in Michigan faces reported axing.
item.content:encoded:
LIV Golf's team championship will reportedly not be taking place this season.

If you've been paying attention to the situation involving LIV Golf, this report of the season finale being canceled should come as no surprise. It also sums up just how dire things have become for the breakaway circuit, while simultaneously contradicting the messaging LIV CEO Scott O’Neil tried to sell to the golf world in June.

According to Flushing It Golf, the team championship in Michigan is expected to officially be canceled after "multiple contractors" told the account that their travel and accommodations have been canceled and that "money is also owed."

TRUMP WEIGHS IN ON LIV GOLF, PGA TOUR AFTER SAUDIS PULL FUNDING OF STARTUP LEAGUE

Flushing It's report comes just days after LIV golfer Martin Kaymer told Today's Golfer that the team championship scheduled for Aug. 27-30 was "highly unlikely" to take place.

LIV Golf was unreachable for comment regarding the report of the team championship being canceled. A source with knowledge of the situation shared with OutKick that LIV continues to have positive discussions with prospective investors for LIV Golf 2.0 while working to secure funding for the circuit's future and long-term sustainability.

PGA TOUR CEO SHARES JARRING COMMENTS ABOUT PLAYERS RETURNING AS LIV GOLF SAUDI FUNDING DISAPPEARS

The LIV team championship was supposed to offer a purse of $40 million, with $11.2 million going to the winning team. However, it is difficult to pay out that type of purse when you presumably have no money.

In April, the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) officially announced that it would be cutting off its funding to LIV Golf. The PIF's statement explained that its funding would remain in place through the remainder of the 2026 season, but that does not appear to be the case with the reported cancellation of the season finale.

This new development of LIV potentially shutting its doors earlier than expected doesn't exactly support the claim O'Neil made during an appearance on CNBC on June 9 in which he hailed the Saudi PIF as an "incredible organization."

"I can say that they've been terrific partners so far," O'Neil began, referring to the Saudis funding LIV Golf. "You have to take an incredible organization like PIF at their word, and they've been very public about funding us through the season. We are full steam ahead, the players are locked in, the management team is locked in."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

It was reported in early 2026 that LIV Golf's net spending per month averaged $100 million in 2024 and 2025. For the 2026 campaign, LIV's fifth, Saudi PIF Governor Yasir Al Rumayyan reportedly approved a $266.6 million capital injection into the circuit.

If the LIV team championship is indeed canceled, it would mark the second LIV event on the original calendar to be axed in 2026. The LIV New Orleans event scheduled for late June was originally postponed in April, and while a targeted date sometime in the fall has been rumored, it seems highly unlikely the circuit makes its way to Louisiana.

LIV's next scheduled event is set for Aug. 6-9 in New York before heading to Indianapolis from August 20-23.

item.title: Tony Romo treating his field sobriety test like an NFL combine leaves fans stunned

item.content:encoded:

The former NFL quarterback was arrested last week following a golf tournament in Wisconsin and charged with an OWI. Romo was initially pulled over for "unsafe passing" on a Milwaukee highway, told the officer he was coming from a golf course and insisted he had consumed "zero" drinks before asking to call his attorney.

TONY ROMO ARRESTED IN MILWAUKEE FOR ALLEGED OWI OFFENSE: REPORT

When asked to step out of the vehicle, the current NFL CBS analyst responded, "Because I'm coming from a golf course, you think I'm drunk?"

Spicy! But, here's where the temp really cranks up ...

Police then detained Romo and transported him to a nearby station to conduct field sobriety tests, which, frankly, look like the hardest tasks in the world to complete, much less pass.

Romo, apparently, did NOT pass them given he was cuffed and detained shortly after, but it wasn't for a lack of trying.

"Sorry, two back surgeries, I need to stand here," Romo said before limbering up in a parking garage last week.

Amazing. Footage later showed Romo after performing the tests, which included the standard 'put one foot in front of the other and walk in a straight line.'

He appeared to do it just fine, but that wasn't the case.

"Did I pass this test?" he asked at one point before getting cuffed. "No I didn't, huh?"

Peak TV from Romo in that parking garage. I've given him a lot of crap over the years for his shtick in the booth, but this reeled me right back in. I've never seen a man get down on start to stretch like he's about to run the 40 before a sobriety test. Never in my life.

Credit to Romo for giving it his all, though. Some folks mail it in. Not Romo. If he's going to start a task, he's going to try and do it to the best of his ability. That's what four-time Pro Bowl quarterbacks do.

You play to win the game. A great man once said that, and it's true in all facets of life — not just sports. Romo's back was against the wall here after being stuffed in the back of a tiny police car on the drive over, and he needed to work up a quick sweat to get the juices flowing before the lights came on.

I get it. The guy had two back surgeries — as he told the other officers — and a slew of other injuries over a 14-year NFL career. You think he can just fire the engines on command anymore? Don't think so.

P.S.: I'm probably gonna take some flack for this, but whatever. I think Romo got railroaded here. He seems fine. I think he passed the tests with flying colors, and they still booked him.

"We did find a couple shooters," the officer told Romo in the garage after searching his car.

"Were they drank?" he asked. "I don't think any of them were drank."

Yeah, this case is far from over.

Romo was eventually cited for first-offense operating while intoxicated and refusing to submit to a chemical test. He was released and is due in court on Sept. 21.

item.title: Trump says US will 'beat the f------ s--- out of them' after Iran launches surprise missile strike

item.content:encoded:

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired ballistic missiles at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base and the headquarters of the U.S. military’s Central Command in Jordan, the paramilitary force said in a statement carried by Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.

We're going to take a page from Livvy Dunne's playbook by making difficult things look easy, or something like that.

The former athlete turned model did some Baywatch promotion on Tuesday on social media with an announcement in the iconic red one-piece. She wrote, "It’s a tough job @baywatch."

Now, because I'm down with the younger generation, I know tough has more than one meaning, and I'm sure that's what Livvy meant. But I'm choosing to turn the viral post into a bit of inspiration here.

RUMORS DEVIN BOOKER AND SUPERMODEL IRINA SHAYK ARE DATING HEAT UP AFTER SUPPOSED SIGHTINGS IN THE HAMPTONS

Livvy's now in the reboot of an iconic show and she's making all of these difficult things look very easy.

Let's get to the emails. There's a victory lap that a few of you out there in Screencaps Nation would like to get to.

SeanJo,

I've never sent meat before so here's our latest spun up chicken. Biggest of the summer at almost six pounds. We've found it's a fairly hassle-free way to have a great meal and it doesn't heat up our non-AC house.

I had a great one-day summer outing in my Bronco with my neighbor who drove his Jeep. Did 100 miles on gravel and sometimes barely there roads over three Idaho mountain passes. SeanJo

We don't judge around here.

- Jim T. in San Diego writes:

Okay, as a forty-year veteran of the news business - reporter, editor, columnist - and someone who taught an upper-division journalism course at a prestigious university, here's what I don't get about this whole ESPN v Outkick v The Athletic situation regarding former on-air talent Ryan Clark:

When Outkick called for comment, reportedly ESPN reached out to a reporter at The Athletic as the ESPN brass apparently dislikes Outkick and preferred The Athletic get the scoop.

And here's where I'm lost.

Isn't ESPN a sports news outlet? And isn't The Athletic are least somewhat competition to ESPN?

Why not have your OWN staff report on it?

I survived numerous rounds of layoffs at the newspaper I worked at longest and, to be fair, our company almost never covered them all that well (although we surely never fed the announcement to a favored competitor!). We'd have a short article the next day announcing the total number of layoffs, and a canned response from the publisher about how valued these employees were. (And his sentiments weren't faked - I knew the publisher, and it tore him up having to let people go. But the advertising model was in free fall and he couldn't spend money he didn't have.)

But I don't believe we ever named those who were let go. That was left to the local alternative outlets, who'd start bombarding everyone at our paper to find out who was let go.

Other papers across the country have done the same: announce the layoffs, not the names.

I get the desire to protect your laid off folks from public embarrassment - getting laid off sucks. Been there, trust me.

But when it is patently obvious that the details ARE going to become public, isn't it better to make that announcement yourself? Take away some of the breathless drama which I'm guessing is even more embarrassing?

If there are actual privacy laws surrounding this so that the company doing the layoffs is legally prohibited from naming names, that I can understand. But I've yet to see anyone ever say that on the record. "We had to eliminate 10 jobs today, but privacy laws prevent us from telling you who they are."

Instead, the competition begins poring over future editions to see which bylines have disappeared. Or, in broadcast, whose shows or slots are gone.

The fact is, under defamation law, anyway (which obviously differs from privacy law), most journalists can be considered limited public figures. They carry influence in their market, and their work can be fairly criticized to a level other professions cannot because journalists are considered to have willingly entered into the public arena in a way, say, a sales executive or mechanic has not.

So Ford not naming the factory workers being laid off makes more sense to me than ESPN not naming the on-air talent whose jobs were eliminated.

Screencaps Nation is large and well-connected - perhaps the 90 percent or more of your readers who are smarter than me can explain this. (For the handful who are NOT smarter than me: Good lord, people, who gets you dressed in the morning?)

item.title: Trump's evolving China rhetoric raises eyebrows over TikTok strategy amid scorching election meddling warning
item.description: Trump's softer tone toward China raises concerns about TikTok's algorithm, which is still under ByteDance control despite the app's new U.S. ownership deal.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is striking a noticeably softer tone toward China just days after delivering a public address to the nation accusing Beijing of "sinister election meddling."

The fresh set of accusations levied on July 16 raised new questions about the Trump administration's posture towards China, especially as it moves to keep TikTok operating in the U.S. while warning against the hostility of the world power against America.

"President Trump just told the nation that China tried to influence the 2020 election and weaken his presidency. During that same year, the intelligence community identified TikTok as a primary vector of CCP influence in the United States," Hudson Institute Senior Fellow Michael Sobolik, who specializes in U.S.–China relations, told Fox News Digital.

"Beijing still controls the algorithm, which means that the very dangers Trump raised persist today," Sobolik added.

TRUMP'S ELECTION INTEGRITY SPEECH: 7 TAKEAWAYS EVERY AMERICAN SHOULD KNOW

Trump has long taken a hard line on China, using tariffs, trade pressure and national security warnings to frame Beijing as one of America's chief adversaries.

In his recent address to the nation, the president accused the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) of running a "sinister" campaign to interfere in U.S. elections and influence Americans and undermine his presidency.

Yet just five days later, on July 21, Trump suggested "China is maybe a little bit different today." It struck a softer tone that falls more in line with the president's backing of a deal to keep TikTok operating in the U.S., despite seeking during his first term and at the start of his second to force the app out over national security concerns.

"The CCP hasn’t changed. Xi Jinping hasn’t changed. But President Trump has," Sobolik detailed.

"He’s much more conciliatory toward China in his second term than he was in his first. He risks telegraphing significant weakness to Xi by letting China off the hook."

Trump downplayed Beijing's past election interference, suggesting both countries engage in similar tactics and indicating he was more focused on future negotiations than revisiting China's actions.

TRUMP’S UPBEAT CHINA MESSAGE COLLIDES WITH DEEPENING BEIJING RIVALRY

"It took place a long time ago. I think China is maybe a little bit different today than it was then," Trump conceded.

"But look there, they do things and we do things to them. I'll be honest — do we do things to them too? It's not a one-way street, but we'll be talking to them," said Trump when speaking about Chinese election meddling days after his "free and fair elections" televised remarks.

Sobolik argued the softened rhetoric could embolden Beijing to continue attempts to influence U.S. politics in the future.

In his first term, Trump sought to ban TikTok, saying it posed a national security risk. Then, during his second term, Trump joined the app, and in recent weeks, so have his top Cabinet members.

"President Trump has saved TikTok for its millions of American users — yet another promise made, promise kept," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital. "With the new TikTok under the control of U.S. investors, Americans can continue to enjoy TikTok with their data fully protected."

TikTok’s ownership deal was reconstructed at the beginning of this year to have majority U.S. ownership while still giving Chinese technology company ByteDance a 19.9% stake – 0.01% below the threshold required under U.S. law.

CHILL COMING FROM TRUMP’S SUMMIT WITH XI IS PROOF OF A NEW COLD WAR WITH CHINA

While the app is based in the U.S., Sobolik said that TikTok's algorithm remains under ByteDance’s control via a licensing regime.

"The fact that it’s training on U.S. data stored on servers in America doesn’t change the fundamental reality that a Chinese Communist Party-controlled company still controls the algorithm itself," said Sobolik. "The administration hasn’t directly addressed the possibility that Beijing could calibrate the app’s algorithm in concerning ways."

Trump visited China in May for a high-stakes summit with President Xi Jinping on several of the biggest pressure points in the U.S.-China relationship — from trade and Taiwan to AI and human rights. Those meetings appeared to end without firm public breakthroughs.

In his final meeting with Xi at the summit, Trump touted what he called "fantastic trade deals."

Sobolik said Trump "wants what he’s always wanted with China," which is a trade deal.

"He needs to think broader and bigger. Economic competition is one part of the larger new cold war that’s playing out between Washington and Beijing," he said.

Sobolik said Trump is placing too much emphasis on trade while overlooking other important areas of competition with China.

"Xi will have the advantage," he added.

Trump said Xi will be visiting the U.S. on Sept. 24, with artificial intelligence expected to be a key topic during their talks.

item.title: Fauci pleads Fifth with 'zero legal justification' as critics erupt and demand contempt charges

Former National Institutes of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Anthony Fauci repeatedly refused to answer substantive questions from Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, leaving the Kentucky Republican frustrated and critics enraged.

RAND PAUL BLASTS FAUCI AS ‘UNCONCERNED WITH LIBERTY', ‘NOT BEING HONEST WITH THE AMERICAN PEOPLE’

Paul argued that Fauci did not have that ability during a congressional investigation conducted under a lawful subpoena, noting that it is a crime under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 to knowingly make false statements to Congress.

"Perfect attorney for the evil elf."

Former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich questioned why Fauci would do so, suggesting congressional testimony is intended to inform the public.

"Interesting. It’s about COVID, public health, & the public’s right to know," Blagojevich said.

Moms for Liberty co-founder Tiffany Justice said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital that Fauci's actions permanently harmed children affected by his pandemic policy recommendations:

"Parents were forced to live with the consequences of Dr. Fauci's decisions every single day. Our kids lost years of learning, friendships, milestones, and opportunities they'll never get back," Justice said.

"Now, when it's time for accountability, he refuses to answer questions under oath. That's infuriating. The American people deserve answers now."

Paul scheduled a contempt vote next week against Fauci, he told reporters after the hearing.

item.title: Storm player wears trans rights shirt ahead of Fever game in stark contrast to Sophie Cunningham’s stance
item.description: Stefanie Dolson wore a "Trans Rights are Human Rights" shirt days after Sophie Cunningham defended biological women in sports, deepening the WNBA divide.
item.content:encoded:
Just days after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham found herself under fire for defending women's sports, Seattle Storm center Stefanie Dolson appeared to offer a statement of her own, arriving for Tuesday night's game wearing a shirt reading "Trans Rights are Human Rights."

On its own, the shirt might have been dismissed as routine WNBA activism. But the timing made it impossible to ignore.

The official Seattle Storm X account quickly endorsed the message, featuring Dolson wearing the shirt across its official social media channels.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTERPROTEST

Tuesday's pregame scene made the league's broader embrace of transgender inclusion impossible to miss while putting Cunningham, one of its few dissenting voices, in the spotlight.

The WNBA has long viewed itself as the vanguard of progressive sports leagues, consistently embracing social activism while leaving little room for dissenting views.

The controversy began after ESPN published a profile on Cunningham in which the Fever guard addressed the backlash she has received for defending women's sports.

Cunningham pushed back on critics who have accused her of being anti-trans.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham said. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

When reporters later asked whether she still stood by those comments, Cunningham didn't waver.

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

"I said what I said," Cunningham told reporters ahead of a recent matchup against the Connecticut Sun. "I think it's kind of common sense." She pointed to Title IX as protecting female athletes.

"It's really important to protect children. And that's little girls who are also involved in that category."

Addressing accusations of bigotry, she added: "I extend love, and I don't dislike anyone... but I'm also there to love biological women. And I think that there are rights that need to be protected."

Within the WNBA, defending biological women has become an increasingly lonely stance.

The WNBA Players Association has publicly supported trans inclusion, while former Fever teammate Brianna Turner has argued that restrictions on biological males distract from broader structural inequities.

Against that backdrop, Cunningham has become one of the league's few prominent players willing to publicly challenge the prevailing view on transgender participation in women's sports.

She has given voice to athletes who argue protecting women's sports is about fairness, not hatred.

Whether intentional or not, Dolson's shirt sharply contrasted with Cunningham's recent comments and reflected the league's broader embrace of transgender inclusion.

"Trans Rights are Human Rights" has become a common rallying cry for pro-trans advocates.

By celebrating Dolson while treating Cunningham's defense of Title IX as controversial, the Storm's official channels highlighted what critics see as a glaring double standard.

The Fever organization attempted to strike a middle ground, issuing a statement noting that its players are "thoughtful adults with their own perspectives and voices."

The contrast couldn't have been clearer. Dolson's message reflected the prevailing stance embraced by many within the WNBA. Cunningham has emerged as one of the league's few active players willing to publicly challenge it.

Cunningham isn't backing down. Neither is the debate over women's sports.

Indiana handily beat Seattle, 105-95.

item.title: New York wants to govern Iowa and Missouri — we're suing to stop it cold
item.description: Iowa and Missouri challenge New York's greenhouse gas reporting rule in federal court, saying it illegally targets out-of-state fuel suppliers.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis famously called the states "laboratories of democracy." In those laboratories, Iowans shape Iowa’s laws, Missourians make Missouri’s laws, and New Yorkers establish New York’s laws. That is a core tenet of federalism — a structural part of our nation’s Constitution that allows for great variation and competition between the states. What a state can’t do, however, is lay claim to the entire country as its laboratory.

That’s exactly what New York is trying to do. Its new greenhouse gas reporting rule requires "fuel suppliers" throughout the nation to register with New York and report information related to greenhouse gas emissions. But the rule doesn’t just concern companies doing business in the Empire State. New York has made clear that its new regulation applies to any ethanol and biodiesel producers whose product may, after being blended or sold by others, eventually end up in New York. In short, New York expects out-of-state producers and distributors to comply with its civil and criminal rules, even if the connection to the state is extremely remote or hypothetical.

This includes producers and distributors in our states — Iowa and Missouri. Together, we represent the nation’s leading producers of ethanol and biodiesel. Our states’ energy economies support millions of farmers, workers, families, and communities. New York’s rule would impose significant compliance costs, reporting obligations, inspections, civil penalties, and even criminal liabilities on businesses operating far from the Empire State.

The issue is not whether New York can create environmental rules for itself: of course it may. Rather, it is whether one state can force citizens, farmers, manufacturers, and businesses in other states to abide by its regulatory program.

Our states have made different policy choices for greenhouse gas regulation. Iowa has not chosen to impose New York-style radical reporting mandates on every fuel producer or supplier. Missouri has similarly refrained from adopting extreme greenhouse gas reporting requirements. Those choices belong to our citizens and their elected representatives. New York may disagree with them, but it cannot override them.

If every state had the right to regulate all others, the result would not be federalism: It would be chaos. Imagine if Iowa sought to regulate how financial institutions operate in New York to counter downstream effects in Iowa, and Missouri sought to regulate technology companies in California for similar reasons.

This sounds crazy, but such regulatory chaos has already started to seep into our federal system. California and Massachusetts regulate how hog farmers around the country operate. California has a greenhouse gas disclosure law requiring large companies doing business there to report emissions and climate-related information, including out-of-state operations and even emissions in the entire supply chain. New York and Vermont have enacted "climate superfund" laws seeking to charge companies for past contributions to alleged climate-related harms. And Boulder, Colorado, claims international energy companies Exxon and Suncor are liable for alleged harms stemming from worldwide greenhouse gas emissions — which the Supreme Court will hear arguments on this fall.

Together, these scenarios reflect a troubling trend: If a policy goal seems big enough, some states think they can reach beyond their borders to solve it.

The Supreme Court has long recognized that one state cannot govern the citizens of another state. Each state is equal under the Constitution, and none has special privileges over any other. That limitation is one of the basic conditions that makes our federal system possible, and New York cannot ignore it.

Federalism protects individual rights. Among other benefits, individuals can remove elected officials who don’t respect their rights by expressing their preferences in legislative and gubernatorial elections — and influencing national laws through their representatives in Congress. And at the state level, federalism provides another powerful mechanism to check government excess. Anyone who doesn’t like a state’s laws and isn’t satisfied with their electoral recourse can move out of that state.
